in_text_mentions: PLE is the commonest photosensitive disorder, characterized by an intermittent eruption of non-scarring pruritic erythematous papules, vesicles or plaques (Figure 1) that develop within hours of ultraviolet radiation (UVR) exposure of patient skin. The disease is dependent on genetic susceptibility, as well as environmental component, such as type of exposure. PLE appears to cluster in families: it has been estimated that the prevalence of PLE was 21 and 18% in monozygotic and dizygotic twins, respectively (1). panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: H&E of spring elbow rash Case 1, article confirms PLE variant by histopathology; panel A shows spared epidermis with superficial and deep perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate at x10. B: Same PLE Case 1 biopsy at x40 showing spared epidermis with superficial and deep perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate. C: High-power x200 view of dermo-epidermal junction of PLE elbow lesion showing lymphocytic infiltrate. D: High-power x200 view showing infiltrate clustered around vessels, consistent with perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate of PLE.

Frontiers in medicine 2023. doi:10.3389/fmed.2023.1260514. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Spring eruption on the elbows. Histopathologic features (Case 1). Haematoxylin-eosin (A) (x10) (B) (x40) (C) (x200) (D) (x200). (A, B) Spared epidermis. Superficial and deep perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate. (C) Respective dermo-epidermal junction. (D) Infiltrate clustered around vessels.
in_text_mentions: In all cases, histological examinations revealed perivascular superficial and deep lymphocytic infiltrates in the dermis, along with variable degrees of dermal edema. Epidermal changes were present in four of the patients, along with mild spongiosis and parakeratosis (Figure 4). The anti-CD123 marker staining was negative for all patients (images not shown).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: Panel A shows spring elbow rash in patient A, from article confirming elbow rash as variant of polymorphous light eruption by photoprovocation; sun-exposed papular eruption with confluent erythematous plaque. B: Panel B self-taken elbow photo showing sun-induced maculopapular eruption in PLE elbow-rash series. C: Panel C self-taken elbow photo showing sun-induced maculopapular eruption in PLE elbow-rash series. D: Panel D shows elbow lesions at first interview, sun-induced maculopapular eruption in PLE elbow-rash series. E: Panel E self-taken elbow photo showing sun-induced maculopapular eruption in PLE elbow-rash series.

panels.figure_caption: Clinical images of spring rash on the elbows in five patients who underwent photobiological studies. Some of the patients' photos (B, C, E) were self-taken before their visit to the hospital. They were asymptomatic during their first visit prior to undergoing photobiological studies. Patients (A, D) presented with some lesions during the first interview, as shown in the images.
in_text_mentions: with phototype III, and one patient with phototype IV. All patients reported a symmetrical, maculopapular, and pruritic skin eruption on the elbows that began in spring within hours/days of sun exposure and disappeared after several days without sun exposure, and topical treatment with corticosteroids was administered in some cases (Table 1; Figure 1). Subsequently, they presented similar recurrent outbreaks that were always related to sun exposure. All the patients studied had previously undergone blood tests, including porphyrins, IgE, and antinuclear antibodies, and the results were normal.
